# YouTube Shorts Script Generator: 36 Hooks and Script Beats You Can Use Today

At 0:02, the viewer has already decided whether to keep watching or swipe. If your YouTube Short opens with “Hey guys” or a long setup, the useful part of your idea may arrive after the decision is made.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you ready-to-use opening lines and simple script beats for common Shorts formats. Use them as raw material, then make the promise specific to your video. A YouTube Shorts script generator is most useful when it turns one topic into several distinct openings, on-screen text options, and a compact structure you can actually film.

## How to make an opening survive the swipe

A strong first line does one job: it gives the viewer a reason to wait for the next line. That reason can take different shapes.

- A contrarian hook challenges a familiar assumption.
- A mistake hook identifies the costly thing the viewer may be doing.
- A question hook makes a precise gap the video will answer.
- A result hook leads with the visible outcome, then earns the explanation.
- A story hook starts at the moment something changed.

Match the hook to what your Short can prove. If the video shows a process, promise the process. If it tells a story, promise the turn. If it gives advice, name the mistake or decision—not a vague “tip.”

## Fitness and wellbeing Shorts

1. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “Stop trying to work out every day.” On-screen: “Daily workouts can backfire”

2. **Mistake** — Spoken: “Your first gym week is probably too hard.” On-screen: “Week-one mistake”

3. **Question** — Spoken: “Why do beginners quit before they see progress?” On-screen: “Why beginners stop”

4. **Result** — Spoken: “This is the [ADD: duration] routine I use when motivation disappears.” On-screen: “[ADD: duration] fallback routine”

5. **Story** — Spoken: “I changed one part of my warm-up, and this is what happened next.” On-screen: “The warm-up change”

6. **Script beat** — 0–3s: “You do not need a perfect plan to restart.” 3–12s: show the smallest version of the workout. 12–24s: explain how to repeat it. 24–30s: ask viewers to save the routine for their next low-energy day.

## Food and cooking Shorts

7. **Result** — Spoken: “This dinner starts with one pan and [ADD: number] ingredients.” On-screen: “One-pan dinner”

8. **Mistake** — Spoken: “Your roasted vegetables are steaming because of this.” On-screen: “Why they go soggy”

9. **Question** — Spoken: “What do you cook when the fridge looks empty?” On-screen: “Empty-fridge meal”

10. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “Do not salt this at the beginning.” On-screen: “Salt later”

11. **Story** — Spoken: “I made this after forgetting to shop, and it stayed in rotation.” On-screen: “Accidental favorite”

12. **Script beat** — 0–3s: reveal the finished dish. 3–8s: name the constraint. 8–22s: show the key steps. 22–30s: show the final texture or cut and state who the recipe is for.

## Personal finance Shorts

13. **Mistake** — Spoken: “Your budget is not failing because you buy coffee.” On-screen: “The budget leak”

14. **Question** — Spoken: “Where did the first [ADD: currency amount] of your month go?” On-screen: “Find the first leak”

15. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “A cheaper subscription is not always the fix.” On-screen: “Not the real problem”

16. **Result** — Spoken: “Here is the [ADD: number]-line check I use before any nonessential purchase.” On-screen: “Purchase check”

17. **Story** — Spoken: “I stopped guessing where my money went and started with this screen.” On-screen: “Start here”

18. **Script beat** — 0–3s: name one spending pattern. 3–10s: show where it hides. 10–22s: offer a small review process. 22–30s: invite viewers to use their own number in the template.

## Productivity and study Shorts

19. **Question** — Spoken: “Why does your to-do list make you avoid work?” On-screen: “Why lists overwhelm”

20. **Mistake** — Spoken: “You are planning tasks at the wrong size.” On-screen: “Shrink the task”

21. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “Do not start your study session with your hardest chapter.” On-screen: “Start differently”

22. **Result** — Spoken: “This is how I turn one vague project into a first [ADD: duration] block.” On-screen: “First work block”

23. **Story** — Spoken: “I kept postponing this task until I rewrote one sentence.” On-screen: “The sentence that helped”

24. **Script beat** — 0–3s: state the friction. 3–10s: show the common response that fails. 10–22s: demonstrate the smaller next action. 22–30s: give a prompt viewers can copy.

## Beauty, style, and home Shorts

25. **Mistake** — Spoken: “This is why your outfit feels unfinished.” On-screen: “The missing detail”

26. **Question** — Spoken: “How do you make a small room look less crowded?” On-screen: “Small-room reset”

27. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “You do not need more storage first.” On-screen: “Not more bins”

28. **Result** — Spoken: “I changed [ADD: number] things on this shelf.” On-screen: “[ADD: number] shelf changes”

29. **Story** — Spoken: “This corner looked awkward until I moved one object.” On-screen: “One-object fix”

30. **Script beat** — 0–3s: show the before. 3–8s: name the visual problem. 8–22s: make the changes in sequence. 22–30s: reveal the after and identify the first change to try.

## Creator, business, and tutorial Shorts

31. **Question** — Spoken: “Why are people leaving your tutorial before the useful part?” On-screen: “Tutorial drop-off”

32. **Mistake** — Spoken: “You explained the tool before showing the outcome.” On-screen: “Show the result first”

33. **Contrarian** — Spoken: “Your next video does not need a better camera.” On-screen: “Fix the opening”

34. **Result** — Spoken: “Here is the [ADD: number]-step setup behind this result.” On-screen: “[ADD: number] steps”

35. **Story** — Spoken: “I knew this tutorial was unclear when the same question kept appearing.” On-screen: “The repeated question”

36. **Script beat** — 0–3s: show the completed result. 3–9s: state the obstacle. 9–22s: demonstrate the decisive steps. 22–30s: say what the viewer should try first.

## Pick the right hook before you write the rest

Choose the hook based on the evidence your video can show in the next few seconds.

If you have a visible before-and-after, use a result hook. If you are correcting a common belief, use a contrarian hook. If the video teaches a repeatable action, use a mistake hook. If the payoff is an explanation, use a sharply bounded question.

Then write the first three seconds as a testable promise. Remove the greeting, the channel introduction, and any sentence that only explains what the video is about. Read the hook aloud once. If it sounds like a title rather than something a person would say, shorten it.

## Test hooks without changing the whole video

Make two openings for the same core video. Keep the subject, footage, and payoff consistent; change only the spoken first line and the on-screen text. One version might name the mistake, while another asks the question.

Watch each version with the sound off. The on-screen text should still establish the subject. Watch it with your eyes closed. The spoken line should still create a clear reason to continue. The better opening is usually the one that reaches the specific problem sooner.

Do not treat every video as the same kind of test. A recipe, a personal story, and a software walkthrough earn attention differently. Keep a small record of which hook type fits each format you make, then generate variations within that format.

## FAQ

### What should a YouTube Shorts script generator create?

Ask for more than a title. Useful output includes a positioning angle, multiple spoken hooks, matching on-screen text, a recommended option, a timed script outline, and a caption idea.

### How long should a YouTube Shorts hook be?

Use only the words needed to state the tension, question, or result. The exact length depends on how quickly the line can be understood aloud and on screen.

### Can I use the same idea for several Shorts?

Yes. Keep the underlying lesson, but test different angles: the mistake, the question, the surprising result, or the story moment that led to the lesson.

### What information should I provide before generating a script?

Include the topic, audience, video length, tone, and the proof or footage you have. Add any constraint that matters, such as “for beginners,” “no voice-over,” or “[ADD: duration] seconds.”

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the kind of brief and structured output you can receive:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
